source.title: AnchorKV: Safety-Aware KV Cache Compression via Soft Penalty with a Refusal Anchor

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper adapts the difference-of-means idea into a key-space harm anchor for a KV-cache compression defense and reports how that method performs. It does not intervene on the residual-stream direction by ablating or adding it, or otherwise test the original causal claim.
record.gate_note: The paper measures harmful-versus-harmless discrimination in key space and reports jailbreak and LongBench outcomes for its compression method. It cites the original residual-stream direction result as background, but does not test residual-stream ablation or addition. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the difference-in-means recipe to build a key-space harm anchor at layer 15 of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. It then reports only that anchor's prompt-classification AUROC and its KV-compression method's ASR and LongBench scores. It never ablates or adds the direction in the residual stream or key space to test whether refusal is mediated by it, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also frame the AUROC result as showing that the linear refusal direction 'extends beyond residual-stream activations' to key space. That reading rests only on discrimination, not on causal tests. They further conclude that at lambda=10 the added utility cost (1.07 points) is smaller than the cost of compression itself (1.59).
record.recipe_differences: The paper adapts the difference-of-means recipe to per-head keys at a selected eviction layer, then uses the anchor to penalize token-retention scores. It does not perform the original residual-stream ablation or addition interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The anchor's discriminative performance varies by layer. The selected layer is 15; layers 15 and 18 are reported as tied on validation AUROC, and the paper says downstream compression results are insensitive to that choice. Jailbreak ASR and LongBench utility vary with penalty strength λ, with a reversal at large λ.

fits_no_version.finding: A difference-in-means anchor in layer-15 key-projection space separates harmful from harmless AdvBench-paraphrase prompts with test AUROC 0.996. The layer profile peaks at middle layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful-versus-harmless information is linearly separable in per-head key space at middle layers (classification, not causal mediation).

fits_no_version.finding: FastKV compression at 25% retention raises AdvPrompter ASR versus FullKV, especially under cross-model transfer (0.299 to 0.632).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aggressive KV-cache eviction can erode refusal under jailbreak attacks.

fits_no_version.finding: Penalizing retention of anchor-aligned tokens lowers ASR (0.68 to 0.13 at lambda=10) at a small LongBench cost. Very large penalties reverse the benefit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A key-space harm anchor used in token selection can reduce jailbreak ASR non-monotonically in penalty strength.

record.problems: The evaluation uses one target model and one anchor-data distribution. The reported AUROC is for harmful-versus-harmless prompt discrimination, not a causal refusal intervention. The ASR evaluation uses keyword or phrase matching to identify refusals; most ASR sweep outcomes are reported with one random seed and without numeric uncertainty. The held-out discrimination test is within the AdvBench-paraphrase distribution, and the paper notes that out-of-distribution discrimination was not directly evaluated.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports per-task LongBench scores across conditions in Table 1; these task-level values are not included because the record keeps the reported 16-task average as the capability summary. The text additionally describes task heterogeneity, including declines on QA-style tasks and the LCC drop at lambda=300, but does not provide enough clearly assigned values in the flattened table excerpt here to add separate task rows.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of the direction, and no measurement of refusal change under intervention. AUROC classification only.
Does not test whether AdvPrompter attacks suppress the direction. No training against ablation.
Multiple or nonlinear anchors are mentioned only as future work.
The anchor is described as harm, but harm and refusal are not separated.
The anchor is built in key space rather than transferred across languages, model variants, or from base to instruct. Only one model is used.
No comparison of training methods or stages.

record.verdict_notes: The direction is used purely as a classifier feature inside a compression defense. The authors' 'validates the refusal direction' language overstates what AUROC shows: no intervention is done on refusal. There is one model, single-seed sweeps, keyword-match ASR, and in-distribution anchor validation only.

versions.untested_parts: Residual-stream direction ablation and addition; whether either changes refusal; whether other abilities remain intact under those interventions.
No weight edit or abliteration is performed.
The study does not test whether attacks suppress the direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
The paper notes that multiple or nonlinear components may be possible, but does not compare them experimentally.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No transfer test across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models; the key-space representation is a different operational space, not one of these transfer settings.
No comparison of refusal training methods or training stages.
